intro: A polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ drawn as the angle sweeps, beside the graph of $r$ against $\theta$. The current point and its distance from the origin are the same orange in both views, so you can see a value of $r$ become a distance along a ray. The shaded bands show where the point moves away from the origin and where it moves toward it. In Interval, a secant line on the graph of $r$ against $\theta$ gives the average rate of change of $r$.
howItWorks:
• Polar to rectangular: $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$; back again, $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$ with $\theta$ chosen in the point's quadrant.
  • Negative r: a point with $r < 0$ is $|r|$ units from the origin on the ray opposite the angle. Both views draw those parts dashed.
  • Distance from the origin is $|r|$. It increases where $r > 0$ and $r$ is increasing, or where $r < 0$ and $r$ is decreasing; it decreases in the other two cases.
  • Average rate of change of $r$ on $[\theta_1, \theta_2]$ is $\frac{r(\theta_2) - r(\theta_1)}{\theta_2 - \theta_1}$, the slope of the secant line on the graph of $r$ against $\theta$, in units of $r$ per radian.
  • Shapes: $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ is a rose with $n$ petals when $n$ is odd and $2n$ when $n$ is even; $r = a + b\cos\theta$ has an inner loop when $|a| < |b|$ and is a cardioid when $|a| = |b|$.
  • Keyboard: on the picture, the arrow keys turn the angle by $\frac{\pi}{24}$ (Shift: $\frac{\pi}{6}$), Home and End go to $0$ and $2\pi$.
